title: Psoriasis (adult): topical, phototherapy and systemic treatment
subject: rheumatology-dermatology
summary: Treat mild disease topically (potent corticosteroid plus a vitamin D analogue), move to narrowband UVB or methotrexate when disease is extensive or uncontrolled, and to biologics when PASI is 10 or more and DLQI above 10 despite conventional therapy. Screen annually for psoriatic arthritis and assess cardiovascular risk.

sections.title: Recognise and assess
items: Well-demarcated red plaques with silvery scale on extensor elbows and knees, scalp, lower back, umbilicus and natal cleft; nail pitting and onycholysis; flexural (inverse) psoriasis has little scale.
Guttate psoriasis: small drop-like papules about 2 to 3 weeks after a streptococcal throat infection, mainly in young people.
Assess severity: body surface area (BSA), PASI, high-impact sites (face, scalp, palms, soles, flexures, genitals, nails) and quality of life (DLQI).
Triggers: streptococcal infection, stress, alcohol, smoking, obesity and drugs (lithium, beta-blockers, antimalarials, withdrawal of systemic glucocorticoid).
Generalised pustular psoriasis or erythroderma (fever, fluid, protein and heat loss): same-day specialist referral, often admission.

sections.title: Comorbidity screening and pre-treatment tests
items: Offer annual screening for psoriatic arthritis with a validated tool such as PEST (it does not detect axial disease), especially in the first 10 years; refer to rheumatology as soon as PsA is suspected.

Severe psoriasis (needing phototherapy or systemic therapy): cardiovascular risk assessment at presentation and every 5 years. Address smoking, alcohol, obesity, diabetes, hypertension, lipids, fatty liver disease and depression.
Before systemic therapy: CBC, liver and renal function, lipids, hepatitis B and C, HIV, latent TB screening (IGRA or tuberculin skin test and chest X-ray), pregnancy test.

sections.title: Topical treatment (first line, NICE)
items: Emollients for all. Trunk and limbs: potent corticosteroid once daily plus a vitamin D analogue (calcipotriol) once daily, applied at different times of day, for up to 4 weeks.

If not controlled after up to 8 weeks: vitamin D analogue alone twice daily. If still not controlled after 8 to 12 weeks: potent corticosteroid twice daily for up to 4 weeks, or coal tar; or combined calcipotriol with betamethasone once daily for up to 4 weeks.
Scalp: potent corticosteroid once daily for up to 4 weeks (shampoo, lotion or gel), removing thick scale first.

Face, flexures and genitals: mild or moderate potency corticosteroid once or twice daily for up to 2 weeks; if inadequate, tacrolimus or pimecrolimus (off-label). Never potent or very potent steroids at these sites.
No very potent steroid continuously for over 4 weeks, or potent steroid for over 8 weeks, at any site; aim for a 4-week break between courses. Review 4 weeks after starting a new topical.

sections.title: Phototherapy and conventional systemic therapy
items: Systemic therapy (NICE) when topicals fail and wellbeing is significantly affected, plus extensive disease (BSA over 10% or PASI over 10), localised disease with major functional impact or distress (severe nails, high-impact sites), or failed phototherapy.
Narrowband UVB 2 or 3 times a week for plaque or guttate psoriasis not controlled with topicals.

Methotrexate is the first-choice conventional systemic: start 5 to 10 mg once weekly, increase gradually to an effective dose, maximum 25 mg weekly. Assess at 3 months on the target dose; stop if PASI falls less than 75% (or less than 50% without a DLQI fall of 5 points).

Ciclosporin first when rapid or short-term control is needed, for palmoplantar pustulosis, or when conception is planned: 2.5 to 3 mg/kg/day, up to 5 mg/kg/day after 4 weeks; not continuously beyond 1 year.
Acitretin for pustular psoriasis, or when methotrexate and ciclosporin fail or are unsuitable; highly teratogenic.
Apremilast (oral PDE4 inhibitor) is a further oral option with no routine blood monitoring (AAD-NPF).

sections.title: Biologic therapy
items: Consider a biologic (NICE) when PASI is 10 or more and DLQI above 10 and conventional systemic therapy and phototherapy have failed, are not tolerated or are contraindicated.

Classes: TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, certolizumab), IL-12/23 (ustekinumab), IL-17 (secukinumab, ixekizumab, brodalumab, bimekizumab), IL-23 (guselkumab, risankizumab, tildrakizumab); biosimilars reduce cost.

Choose by comorbidity: TNF or IL-17 inhibitor when psoriatic arthritis is significant; avoid IL-17 inhibitors in inflammatory bowel disease; avoid TNF inhibitors in demyelinating disease or advanced heart failure.
Screen TB and hepatitis B and C before starting; vaccinate beforehand and avoid live vaccines. Assess response at 12 to 16 weeks (PASI 75, or PASI 50 with a DLQI fall of 5 or more).

sections.title: Pregnancy, children and flares
items: Pregnancy: methotrexate and acitretin are contraindicated; emollients, topical corticosteroid and narrowband UVB can be used; ciclosporin or certolizumab when systemic therapy is unavoidable (specialist).

Acitretin: avoid pregnancy during treatment and for 3 years after stopping. Methotrexate: effective contraception for men and women during treatment and for the period after stopping stated in the product information.
Refer children and young people with psoriasis to a specialist at presentation.
Avoid systemic glucocorticoid for psoriasis: withdrawal can precipitate pustular or erythrodermic flares.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Missing psoriatic arthritis (dactylitis, enthesitis, inflammatory back pain, nail disease) until joint damage has occurred.
Potent steroids on the face or flexures (atrophy, striae), or continuous very potent steroid use.
Methotrexate taken daily instead of weekly, or with trimethoprim or co-trimoxazole.
Ignoring cardiovascular risk, depression and alcohol misuse in severe psoriasis.

drugs.name: Calcipotriol 50 micrograms/g
drugs.dose: Apply once or twice daily; maximum 100 g per week in adults
drugs.notes: Irritant on face and flexures; hypercalcaemia with excessive use.

drugs.name: Calcipotriol with betamethasone dipropionate
drugs.dose: Apply once daily for up to 4 weeks (gel or ointment)
drugs.notes: Body and scalp; not face or flexures.

drugs.name: Betamethasone valerate 0.1% (potent)
drugs.dose: Apply once daily for up to 4 weeks
drugs.notes: Maximum 8 weeks continuous; not face, flexures or genitals.

drugs.name: Methotrexate
drugs.dose: Start 5 to 10 mg orally once weekly; increase gradually to effective dose, maximum 25 mg once weekly
drugs.notes: With folic acid; weekly only. Monitor CBC, liver and renal function; liver fibrosis monitoring (for example PIIINP or elastography).

drugs.name: Ciclosporin
drugs.dose: 2.5 to 3 mg/kg/day orally in 2 divided doses; up to 5 mg/kg/day after 4 weeks if needed
drugs.notes: Maximum 1 year continuous. Reduce or stop if BP rises or creatinine rises more than 25% above baseline.

drugs.name: Acitretin
drugs.dose: 25 to 30 mg orally daily initially, then 25 to 50 mg daily according to response
drugs.notes: Teratogenic for 3 years after stopping; monitor lipids and liver function.

drugs.name: Apremilast
drugs.dose: Titrate over 5 days to 30 mg orally twice daily
drugs.notes: Diarrhoea, nausea, weight loss, low mood.

drugs.name: Adalimumab
drugs.dose: 80 mg subcutaneously once, then 40 mg every 2 weeks starting 1 week later
drugs.notes: Screen TB and hepatitis first; review response at 16 weeks.
